Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Can the minister say whether a meeting of the continuing committee dealing with food for peace which on May 7 the minister announced

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minisier of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: FOOD FOR PEACE CONFERENCE
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, the committee was called together in Washington. The Leader of the Opposition asked this question of me just the other day. I thought I had the reply available to give him this morning, but I do not locate it in my papers. I propose giving a report on that matter; perhaps I might do that tomorrow.

subtopic: FOOD FOR PEACE CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have located the answer I mentioned just a minute ago. The Leader of the Opposition asked me a question on June 24 with regard to the Washington meeting on the export of surplus farm products. The wheat utilization committee established by the food for peace conference, on which I reported to the house on May 7 last, held its first meeting on June 15-17 in Washington.
Membership of the committee comprises Argentina, Australia, Canada, France and the United States. The FAO is represented in an observer adviser capacity. The representation at this meeting was at the same level as the preministerial meeting of senior officials held last April. The Canadian delegation on this occasion was led by Mr. John H. English, deputy minister of trade and commerce, and included officials from the departments of trade and commerce, agriculture, finance and external affairs and from the Canadian wheat board.
The purpose of this meeting was chiefly organizational. The principal outcome was the establishment of procedures for the operations of the committee, and guide lines concerning concessional sales of wheat to apply in the selection of recipient countries and the determination of minimum commercial quotas.
Possible schemes of market development and the setting up of national food reserves were also discussed. In this connection a working group at the embassy level was appointed to study and report on these two items for consideration at the next meeting of the committee.
The administrative procedures of the committee were left simple and flexible. The office of the administrator of the U.S. foreign agricultural service will serve as a permanent focal point of contact. The committee will normally convene in the spring and fall of each year at a place to be decided by the committee.
It is expected that the next meeting of the committee will be held next fall in Washington.

Oh, yes, Mr. Speaker. All these matters were under consideration. One of the great values of this wheat utilization committee is that there will be close consultation with regard to all matters dealing with the disposal of surplus food. There will be an avoidance of difficulties among exporting nations when this knowledge is available to them, and available in advance. I think nothing but good is going to come from the meetings of this committee. That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Maritime Coal Production Assistance Act to extend the application of the act to coal producers in all parts of Canada; to provide that the aggregate principal amount of loans made to coal producers under section 6 of the act shall be increased from ten to twenty million dollars and that the aggregate principal amount of loans made to any one coal producer under the same section shall be increased from seven and one-half to twelve million dollars; to extend the operation of the act from the 31st day of October, 1959 to the 31st day of October, 1964; and to authorize certain amendments to the agreement made under the act with the Dominion Coal Company Limited for the purpose of varying the terms of repayment of principal and interest as provided under section four thereof.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS EXTENDING APPLICATION, INCREASING AMOUNTS OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the resolution submitted states, in brief, that it is expedient to extend the provisions of the existing Maritime Coal Production Assistance Act by an amendment to that legislation.
The Maritime Coal Production Assistance Act was studied and passed by parliament in 1949, and provided a fund of $10 million that could be advanced to coal producers in the Atlantic provinces in the form of interest bearing loans to be spent to increase the efficiency of coal production by means of mechanization. The act provided that no loans could be made after October 31, 1959 which, in effect, limited the period to 10 years.

Under this act the operators have been given the opportunity of obtaining loans that might not have been readily available from the usual financial sources. Those who have negotiated loans have also benefited from the special depreciation allowances on the capital cost set out in the act. Since the inception of the act 15 loans have been approved to various coal operators, in the amount of $9,997,101, thus using practically all the funds allotted under the legislation. Of the 15 loans, five have been repaid in full and all others are in good standing as to repayments of capital and payment of interest to May 31, 1959 under the terms of the agreement covering each loan. These loans have all borne interest at rates approved by the Minister of Finance.
Annual reports with respect to the operations under this legislation have been submitted to parliament. The last report covering the operations for the year ending March 31, 1959 was tabled on Monday, April 13, and members will find full details therein of the position of the fund at the close of the fiscal year.
This legislation has been a distinct success in its assistance to coal operators. While costs of producing coal have risen along with costs in all other phases of industry, the help given by the mechanization projects financed under the act has had the effect of increasing the efficiency of mining coal, with the result that the increases in cost have not been as great as they would have been without this help.
The operation of this act has been closely followed by the Dominion Coal Board, and the board have recommended (a) that the provisions of the present act should be extended for a further period of 10 years; (b) that since the funds provided have been exhausted, a further $10 million be made available, and (c) that the assistance be made available to all coal producers in Canada. It is therefore proposed to introduce an amendment to the present legislation which will:
1.	Make it a national act so it will apply to all coal mine operators in Canada;
2.	Increase the aggregate amount of loans that may be made by another $10 million;
3.	Extend the time limit by five years to October 31, 1964;
4.	Increase the amount which may be loaned to one operator from $7,500,000 to $12,000,000.
The amendments proposed will also provide authority for a revision of the agreement made under the act between Her Majesty and the Dominion Coal Company Limited. Representations were made by the company last year for some changes in the schedule set out in the agreement of repayments on their loan of $7,500,000. These representations were

Maritime Coal Production Assistance Act considered, and it was deemed advisable under existing circumstances to alter the schedule of repayments under the agreement. This revision will:
1.	Allow the company to make no further repayments until June 30, 1963, at which time they will again commence repayment at six month intervals based on 30 cents per net ton of production.
2.	Increase the interest rate to 4 per cent per annum from 3J per cent per annum as from July 1, 1957.
In 1957 Bill No. C-54 was introduced authorizing amendments to the original act, intending to meet the representations made by the company. This bill was passed by this house on August 18, 1958. Unfortunately the provisions of this amendment did not fully cover the difficulties, and it remains necessary to clarify the matter by further amendment. The proposed revision provides that the total loan to this company will be fully repaid by June 30, 1970, as set out in the terms of the legislation.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I would repeat my earlier statement that this legislation has been of great assistance to our coal producers in modernizing their methods, in promoting stability in production, and in helping Canadian coal to meet the intensified competition from other fuels. It is our belief that the extension of the assistance in time, in funds, and particularly to all operators across Canada, is timely and will be of even greater benefit to the industry.

Mr. Chairman, we of the official opposition have followed with interest the statement just made by the minister in introducing the legislation having to do with amending the Maritime Coal Production Assistance Act.
As was stated by the minister, the purpose of the present amendments to the Maritime Coal Production Assistance Act is first to extend the application of the act to coal producers in all parts of Canada. Mr. Chairman, we welcome this change, which has been made necessary by the present position of the coal market in this country. I would like the minister to tell us before this resolution is passed if it is the intention of the government to change the name of this act, or will it remain under the name of the Maritime Qoal Production Assistance Act? The minister has stated that the act will now be applicable to Canada as a whole, and 1 wonder if it is the intention of the government to change the name of the act.
The minister has also stated that the purpose of this amendment is to increase from $10 million to $20 million the fund made available for loans under this act. As the minister has stated, this act has been beneficial to the coal industry. It has made

Maritime Coal Production Assistance Act possible the modernization of our coal mines which in turn has made it possible to increase production without a corresponding increase in cost.
In answer to a question I asked in this house on February 23, 1959 we were given the details of the loans made under the present act, and as the minister has said five of these loans have been repaid in full. I may note at this point that four of these loans which have been repaid were made to coal producers in the province of New Brunswick.
I also note that it is the intention of this amendment to make it possible for any one coal producer to increase his loan from $7,500,000 to $12,000,000. I presume that the purpose of this amendment is to make possible a further loan to the Dominion Coal Company for the purchase of a washing plant. I hope the Dominion Coal Board will see fit to recommend to the government that such a loan be granted. It is urgently needed by the company concerned in order to make it possible for this company to compete in the coal market.
The amendment to this act which we are asked to pass will also, as the minister has stated, include a further amendment to the present legislation. We know that this act was amended in 1958, but apparently there was an omission at that time in that the government or those who prepared the amendment failed to realize that the loan made to the Dominion Coal Company could not be extended under the existing terms of the act. We will definitely support the amendment which will make possible the extension of the present loan.
Mr. Chairman, the minister has made it clear that this legislation has been a distinct success in providing assistance to coal operators. This is legislation which was introduced by the previous administration. It has been of great benefit to the coal producers of this country and, as I said at the outset, we of the official opposition will be pleased to support this bill. Before this resolution is passed, however, the minister might inform the house if any further action has been taken following the announcement by the Prime Minister on March 17, when he said that a thorough study of the long term market prospects for coal was urgently required and that meetings were to be held with the government of Nova Scotia and the coal companies concerned. I hope the minister is now in a position to inform the house what action is being taken in this regard.
We in the official opposition realize the importance of this amendment, also, inasmuch as it is likely to benefit the marketing of [Mr. Robichaud.l

coal in this country. It is unfortunate that coal production has decreased very substantially during the month of May, as shown by figures recently released by the dominion bureau of statistics. In fact Canadian coal output slumped 32 per cent in May, to 562,000 tons from 823,114 tons a year earlier, according to these figures. Moreover, this decrease in the production of Canadian coal took place during a period when landed imports were 21 per cent higher, at 1,308,543 tons as against 1,079,754 tons in May of last year. I hope the minister and the government will look into this matter very seriously, as it may have a very serious effect on the marketing of Canadian coal.
We shall wait until we see this bill, but I repeat that on this side of the house we will support it in principle and do everything in our power not to delay its passage.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS EXTENDING APPLICATION, INCREASING AMOUNTS OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
We in the C.C.F. group also support this resolution, but would like to point out several things which we think are missing. First of all, this is the second time in a period of a year when the Maritime Coal Production Assistance Act has been amended, and I think this is another example of Conservative policy with regard to all matters of major importance; no consideration has been given to the long term problems involved and no care has been taken to relate this bill to other acts which are similar in character. For example, a short while ago we passed a national energy act and this present bill, which is concerned with coal production, should obviously come within the scope of that act.
The present amendment adds another $10 million to the fund available under the act, which was set up to assist coal production in the maritime provinces and to help modernize mining equipment. We are pleased that the minister has seen fit to extend this assistance to all Canada, but unless the bill is extended in scope and further amended it can never become a national fuel act and can play no part in any Canadian national fuel policy. We suggest that the minister should consider setting up a national fuel production board which would concern itself with all forms of fuel and come within the scope of the national energy act. However, we welcome the decision to make this additional money available, because mining conditions in the maritimes are becoming increasingly more difficult and the need for improved and more modern machinery to take care of deep and dangerous mining conditions is constantly increasing.
We welcome also the decision to make this act national in coverage, because these same problems are arising in all the coal production areas of this country. We think the $20

million which is now to be available will probably be sufficient to modernize the remaining mines in Canada, but once again I urge the minister to give serious consideration to setting up a national fuel board and bringing this and other acts of a similar nature within the jurisdiction of that board so they might be studied in the light of a national fuel policy which would take into consideration all the forms of energy available to us so these resources could be utilized in the best possible way to the advantage of the Canadian people.

There was a question asked by the hon. member for Gloucester about the name of the new act. This new act will be named the Coal Production Assistance Act. We thought it would be fitting to change the name. A question was also asked about the amendment which is being made to the act, and if I remember well it was about the maximum loan now to be permitted. In the event that a loan is granted to the Dominion Coal Company we must extend the maximum to $12 million, because the first loan granted to the company was $7,500,000 and if the act were not amended the highest loan which could be granted would remain at $7,500,000. That is why we wish to amend the act. Under the first act, the maximum was $7,500,000, and so, in order that this loan may go through, if it does go through, we must raise the limit from $7,500,000, to $12 million.
The other questions will be answered when the bill is discussed. I thank the hon. member for Timiskaming for his suggestion, which will be studied and considered. That is all I have to say at the present time.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CHANGING VALUE OF POUND IN RELATION TO INTERNATIONAL KILOGRAM

the second reading of Bill No. S-20, to amend the Length and Mass Units Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I have just a short statement to make with regard to this very small amendment. The Length and Mass Units Act is chapter 164 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952. This act was passed in 1951. At that time the hon. member for Ottawa West gave a learned discourse to the house on what is a highly technical subject. For those who would be interested in reading that discussion it may be found at page 3474 of Hansard for May, 1951.
In the act the Canadian yard and the Canadian pound were related to the international metre and the international kilogram. This did away with the necessity of having specific physical copies representing the Canadian yard and the Canadian pound. This action had two main advantages; the Canadian weights and measures system was tied directly to the most satisfactory international system of measurement, and the most permanent standards of length and mass in the world became the basis of the Canadian units of measurement.

Length and Mass Units Act
The ratio defining the Canadian pound was taken as the original conversion factor relating both the United Kingdom pound and the United States pound to the kilogram. However, in 1951 it was recognized that the English pound had decreased somewhat in size, creating a difference between it and the United States pound. At that time it could not be foreseen what ratio would be chosen by the United Kingdom and the United States to unify their two pounds. In using the originally accepted ratio relating the pound to the kilogram in the 1951 legislation the need for later revision of the act was foreseen when the United Kingdom and the United States reached agreement.
Over the last three or four years discussions have taken place among these countries to endeavour to resolve the existing differences. A major part in those discussions has been carried on by Dr. L. E. Howlett of the national research council of Canada. An agreement was reached and announced on January 1, 1959 relating to the international yard and the international pound and giving the figures. The international yard equals .9144 metre and the international pound equals .45359237 kilogram. This then necessitated a change in the Length and Mass Units Act altering the last two figures after the decimal point from 43 as now appears in the act to 37. No change is required for the yard-metre ratio but this slight alteration is required for the relationship of the pound-kilogram. The change is significant only in measurements of the highest precision, and does not affect ordinary commerce and industry.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the legislation with which we are dealing is of highly important significance to those working in certain types of advanced scientific work, but has no significance in ordinary trade and commerce. I think it is well to draw to the attention of the house a little of the background of the legislation.
Canada's units of measurement of length and mass had been governed by the weights and measures legislation. We had accepted the standards which we obtained from the British government in 1873. It is interesting to observe that by 1951 the variation in the standards concerned were of such significance as to be important in certain advanced scientific work. It is an indication of the development of this field in Canada and indeed an indication of the development in some of the advanced technology in our production field arising out of developments subsequent to the war that such fine adjustments became of significance.

In 1951 the standards were taken out of the Weights and Measures Act and a separate act was created defining those standards in terms of the international metre and kilogram, and also providing in the Weights and Measures Act that our Canadian national research council should be charged with maintaining our Canadian unit for industrial and trade purposes.
I was glad to hear the minister acknowledge what I and I think all hon. members who have studied this subject will regard as the very splendid work being done in this field by the national research council division headed by Dr. Howlett. It is outstanding work and the type of work of which I think the Canadian government and the Canadian people will be proud.
The actual legislation itself, as I understand it, involves agreement among a great many of the trading countries in the world as to this more precise measurement. In 1951 we did not have that final agreement bringing in the main, the United States and the United Kingdom governments and ourselves together on the precise unit. As I understand this legislation, we now have that agreement and the legislation merely puts in legislative form the result of that agreement. Actually, as I understand it, it reduces the weight of our pound by six one hundred millionths of a kilogram. I think that is the correct way of expressing it.
It will be seen that reduction is of scientific significance only. However, it is interesting that over the 80 years during which we were on the other standard in this respect there was a variation in the British standard bar but during that time there was practically no variation in the international metre. It is one of those things which are perhaps easy for the scientist to explain but which are rather difficult for the layman like myself to follow.
There is, of course, an advantage in this legislation, namely that of getting a scientifically accurate unit. There is also a further advantage in that this indicates that we have obtained international agreement among many nations on this subject. I should be glad if the minister, in his closing remarks, would indicate the countries which will be adopting this standard. I think there are some seven or eight of them, as was indicated in the other place.

Mr. Speaker, the minister will allow me to say a few words in French in connection with the metric system about which I asked a question a few moments ago because there was brought to my attention a recommendation submitted at the convention of the Canadian Association of Geographers in May 1958, which favoured the adoption of the metric system by geographical and geological organizations in Canada. I would like to make a few brief remarks in connection with that recommendation and read the resolution without, I am sure, in the least delaying the passing of this bill.
According to my information:
The metric system has the incomparable advantage, from the scientific and practical points of view, to be the only one based on the decimal system of which all geometrical, electrical, calorific, mechanical, optical and mass units as well as their sub-units logically derive from one another and are interrelated on the aforesaid basis by decimal multiples and sub-multiples.
Hence, because of its very clarity, consistency and efficiency, the metric system has, since its creation in 1801, rapidly become the most popular system of measurement in the world. It is now applied in the whole of Europe (except for the British Isles); in all countries of Central and South America (except for a few islands, or English and American zones); in most of the more important Asiatic countries, among which Japan since April 1951, India since June 1957, the Philippines, Indonesia, Indochina, without mentioning China, which

is about to decide to adopt it; in all French, Spanish, Portuguese, Belgian and independent territories of Africa, save the English colonies.
As a matter of fact, it is significant in this respect that former English colonies like India and the Sudan, Palestine (Israel and Jordan) should have officially adopted the metric system as soon as they became independent.
Thus, not only is the metric system in current use by more than 11 billion people, that is more than 60 per cent of the entire world population of 21 billion people, but it is also gaining ground every year. Even in countries traditionally attached to the English system, the metric system has become practically the only one in use and recognized by most scientific branches such as medicine and pharmacology; botany, zoology, paleontology and crystallography; astrophysics and globe physics,
mineralogy, geology, oceanography and glaciology,_
as an example in this field, the Journal of Glaciology of London has adopted the metric system as the only official one in its pages,-meteorology,- temperature readings by radio observation are given the world over in centigrade degrees. Finally, in the military field, in May 1957, the American army decided to adopt the metric system to be on a par with most of the great armies of the world.
Finally is it necessary to emphasize that all measurements related to research work carried out under the international geophysical year programme will be published by all nations without exception in the metric system only.
In view, on the one hand of the superiority of the metric system in that it is the only system whose units in every class or category and in their relationships are all based on decimals and, on the other hand, of all the mentioned facts concerning its more and more exclusive use and establishing It as the only scientific system of measurement which IS truly universal, it is suggested that all members of the Canadian Association of Geographers as well as all scientific bodies represented there, accept the principle of henceforth submitting in the metric system all measurements involved in their work or at least of writing them down together with their English system equivalents.
1.	To provide for wider circulation and immediate understanding in international scientific circles, of works published in Canada, thus avoiding tiresome measurement adjustments to readers of such works.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO DELETE REFERENCE TO GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA, TO EXTEND APPLICATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. S-22 to amend the Export Credits Insurance Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I have a statement to make which will last about 12 minutes. If you would permit me to continue past one o'clock I should be able to complete it.
The purpose of the proposed amendment is to enable the Export Credits Insurance Corporation, when authorized by the governor in council, to provide direct guarantees to lenders for export transactions and to buy, sell and make loans on guaranteed export paper. I think it might be helpful if I were to review briefly how the corporation operates, what it does, and what its experience has been. The corporation's main function is to insure Canadian exporters against non-payment by foreign buyers of goods and services. It in effect insures the foreign account receivable. The corporation is also authorized to insure sales of Canadian-produced goods by foreign subsidiaries of Canadian companies, and goods shipped on consignment or for exhibition purposes.
This insurance is provided by the government because there are no private commercial concerns offering similar protection. In all other countries where export credits insurance is available a similar service is
Export Credits Insurance Act provided by the government or with government backing. The corporation insures against risks of non-payment by foreign buyers.
These risks are by no means inconsiderable.	The corporation insures both consumer goods sold on short credit terms extending to 30, 60 and 90 days, and also capital goods where payments may be spread over a number of years. One of the basic principles of insurance is that there be a broad spread of risk. Accordingly the corporation generally requires its policyholders who export consumer goods to insure all their export sales made during a twelvemonth period, excluding sales made to the United States of America or sales made against irrevocable letters of credit. In the case of capital goods an individual policy is issued to cover the specific contract of sale.
The provision of export credits insurance in no way subsidizes the exporter, for he pays an appropriate premium for the insurance protection and still has to compete in the markets of the world on the basis of quality, price, credit terms and services rendered. In considering applications for insurance the board of directors of the corporation must exercise reasonable prudence and cannot take on liabilities in any one foreign country which may be too high in relation to the corporation's capital, which is $20 million, or in relation to the credit standing of the importer or the importing country. However, where the board of directors is of the opinion that the insurance would impose on the corporation a liability for a term or an amount in excess of that which the corporation would normally undertake in relation to any one contract, exporter, commodity or country, and the transaction is deemed to be in the national interest, the governor in council may authorize the corporation to insure under section 21 of the act.
The recently tabled annual report of the corporation gives a clear and detailed statistical summary of the corporation's operations and experience. Since the first policy was issued in 1945 export sales of $680 million have been insured, including $215 million authorized under section 21. Claims of $9.6 million have been paid and recoveries of $6.6 million have been obtained. Net claims and operating expenses to December 31, 1958, totalled $4.2 million. Premiums of $4.3 million have been received, so that over the past 14 years the corporation has operated on an almost exactly break-even basis with a surplus on operations of only $136,000. The interest on invested capital,

Export Credits Insurance Act which amounted to $3.6 million, makes up the bulk of the underwriting reserve which now stands at $3.7 million.
One of the problems involved in export trade is that of financing. An exporter of general commodities who sells his goods on short credit terms extending to perhaps 90 days as a rule has no difficulty arranging financing. Financing for such exports is readily available from the chartered banks. With the backing of an export credits insurance policy an exporter can often arrange for an increase in his line of credit or for accommodation on more favourable terms, since he can assign to his bankers the proceeds of any loss payable under his policy. The bank knows that if a foreign bill is not met by the buyer the corporation will have to pay under the policy.
In the case of capital goods, however, particularly where sales to underdeveloped countries are concerned, financing is more of a problem. Manufacturers of heavy equipment selling to domestic buyers in Canada are accustomed to receiving payment in cash on delivery, with the buyer obtaining his funds in the capital market or from financial institutions. In less developed countries it is frequently impossible for the buyer to finance domestically his imports of capital goods, because the local financial institutions and capital market are themselves underdeveloped and because many of these countries suffer from a chronic shortage of foreign exchange. Sales may be possible only if the supplier offers credit. For heavy equipment the credit period required often runs to a matter of years. The need for credit for the foreign buyers and the willingness of competing suppliers to grant extended credit terms obliges the Canadian exporter to sell on similar terms if he hopes to win orders.
With the backing of export credits insurance the Canadian chartered banks have generally found it possible to finance the capital goods business of Canadian exporters. However, it is reported that on some occasions chartered banks have found it difficult to provide the financing required by Canadian exporters, partly because of other commitments on the part of the banks, partly because of the size of the loans, or the terms required. In most countries of the world which are exporters of capital goods there are government facilities in addition to export credits insurance to assist in capital goods financing. Assistance provided by these government institutions includes the provision of either unconditional guarantees or rediscount facilities, or a combination of both.
It is now proposed that the Export Credits Insurance Act be amended to provide similar facilities to Canadian exporters of capital
	. j _! 'H
goods. Accordingly the proposed amendments would empower the government to authorize the export credits insurance corporation to give direct guarantees to lenders covering export transactions, and to buy and sell guaranteed instruments, and to lend money on the security of these guaranteed instruments in a manner similar to the arrangements provided by section 11 of the National Housing Act.
The corporation will administer the new facilities, acting as an agent of the government of Canada and directed by instruction of the governor in council, in the same manner as it now operates under section 21 of the act.
The new facilities will help to provide Canadian exporters of capital goods with export credits on terms broadly similar to those available to exporters in other countries. In this connection, the government is keeping in touch with the export credit terms being offered elsewhere through its missions abroad, and more particularly through the membership of the Export Credits Insurance Corporation in the Berne union. The union is an organization composed of credit insurers representing most of the major capital goods exporting countries. It provides a forum in which the export credits insurance practices of member countries can be reviewed and kept in line with one another.
The house will be interested to know that at the recent 16th annual general meeting of the Berne union held in Amsterdam on June 12 of this year, Mr. H. T. Aitken, who is the head of our export credits insurance corporation, was elected president of the Berne union, which is a compliment to him and an honour to Canada.
The direct guarantees proposed under the amendment will be applicable both to those transactions which are insurable by the corporation under section 13 or by the corporation upon instruction of the governor in council under section 21. The guarantees will be applicable to export paper issued in connection with contracts involving the export of goods or services for amounts of not less than $250,000, approximately, and involving payment periods of at least two years. Guarantees will be unconditional and cover the financed portion of the export contract, normally not more than 80 per cent of the contract price. The guarantees will be effective only after delivery of the goods by the exporter and acceptance of the goods by the buyer.
These guarantees may be provided in the currency of the contract of sale. Sales of capital goods, particularly to Latin American countries, are as a rule in United States dollars. It is felt that the provision of

guarantees in that currency would assist the exporter very materially in his financing arrangements.
Generally these transactions would be covered during the predelivery period by an export credits insurance policy, which policy would become superseded by the guarantee after delivery of the goods by the exporter and acceptance by the buyer. An important feature of the guarantee provision is that it should permit exporters to obtain non-recourse financing from lenders. This arrangement in turn should make it possible for exporters to finance a larger volume of business. In providing unconditional guarantees the corporation will be taking on added risks. An appropriate fee will be charged to cover these added risks.
It is proposed that the guarantees may be extended to all lenders, not only commercial banks. Further, it is proposed that the corporation be empowered to endorse the guaranteed export paper in order to enhance its negotiability.
In addition to the guarantees the proposed amendment would permit the corporation, when authorized by the governor in council, to purchase instruments guaranteed by it, lend money to the holder of a guaranteed instrument upon the security thereof, and sell a guaranteed instrument to any person. It is felt that the provision of such authority will assist in making funds more readily available to Canadian exporters of heavy equipment.
Under section 21 of the present act the liability of the corporation under contracts of insurance issued and outstanding at any time is limited to $200 million. The proposed amendment does not involve any change in this sum. The aggregate of the liability of the corporation under insurance policies issued under section 21 and of all the guarantees issued under the proposed amendments is not to exceed the limit of $200 million presently authorized. It is expected that a greater volume of export business will be facilitated by the new provisions, but individual guaranteed transactions will not increase total liabilities outstanding since when a guarantee becomes effective, an insurance policy is replaced.
Finally, as is the case under the present act, all orders in council made under the proposed amendment would be laid before parliament.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO DELETE REFERENCE TO GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA, TO EXTEND APPLICATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Export Credits Insurance Act, which it is proposed to amend by the bill now before us for second reading, is undoubtedly one of the most important acts we have in force affecting our trade; and bearing in mind the importance of our foreign trade in the general prosperity of the country it is indeed a most important matter for all Canadians. The bill seeks to add to the act a wholly new principle. The act, as hon. members know, provides for the insurance of contracts for payment with respect to the export of goods from this country. There are certain other subsidiary items like services and so on that may also be insured.
The bill before the house provides for the crown through the corporation to buy and sell guaranteed instruments and to guarantee instruments used in the export of products from Canada. There is, of course, a great need for helping the export industry to finance its business. That is undoubtedly a great need in the export trade field today and one which should be met. So we start with a very important piece of legislation being amended and an important step being taken to meet a need that in my opinion is urgent in our commercial world today.
But before discussing the bill in detail I want to raise a preliminary matter that I think should be raised. Under the act it is provided that the limit of liability of the crown is $200 million with respect to the insurance contracts provided for in the act. Under the bill provision is made for doing three things. The first is to guarantee the payment of an instrument given by an importer to an exporter. This is the guarantee factor. The second is the purchase of guaranteed instruments, and the third is the sale of guaranteed instruments.
I have two points I wish to raise. One is that while under the act there is a ceiling limite of $200 million with respect to the relevant clause of the act which provides for

Export Credits Insurance Act insurance by the corporation with the approval of the governor in council, the purpose of the guarantee is a wholly new purpose, and under the liability which is being created by clause 5 of the bill now before us in what will be section 21B of the new act the liability of the importers under all outstanding guaranteed instruments is limited so that the total liability shall not at any time exceed $200 million.
My first point is that this is a wholly new purpose for which possible liability may be incurred or a charge may be made on public funds. The second point is that the bill provides for three separate purposes. The first is a guarantee of instruments, and there is a limit which is the same as the limit under the insurance provisions in the existing act. In addition, however, there is the necessary buying and selling of the guaranteed paper and that buying and selling operation has no limit whatever. It is possible over a period of years to have bought paper to the amount of hundreds of millions of dollars. In other words the limitation of $200 million in the bill is only a limitation on the outstanding guaranteed instruments, but there is no limitation whatever on the losses in the buying and selling or the amount of the buying and selling. It would be possible over a period of years, depending on how quickly guaranteed instruments are replaced, to buy say $1 billion worth of paper, and it is theoretically possible to have a loss of $1 billion. I use that theoretical illustration to make my point. I do not suggest for a minute that there is a probability of that happening at all, but I wanted to make that point.
For these two reasons I am at a loss to understand why the bill was not preceded by a resolution and introduced in the House of Commons rather than being introduced in the other place. In that connection I think I can content myself with reading section 54 of the British North America Act, which is in these words:
54. It shall not be lawful for the House of Commons to adopt or pass any vote, resolution, address, or bill for the appropriation of any part of the public revenue, or of any tax or impost, to any purpose that has not been first recommended to that house by message of the Governor General in the session in which such vote, resolution, address, or bill is proposed.
The significance, of course, of having a resolution is that there is an opportunity for a further committee stage. My point is that the bill provides for the appropriation of a part of the public revenue to a purpose that has not been first recommended to the house by a message from the Governor General. Second, if it is held that bill does not provide for expenditure for a new purpose, then my


further point is that there is an increased liability created by the bill. I thought I should properly raise that preliminary point so that our rights in this important constitutional matter would be preserved and not eroded through any oversight.
Dealing with the substance of the bill itself, I think it is well for us to recall a little of the history of the legislation on this subject. In 1944 the Export Credits Insurance Act was first passed by parliament, having been introduced by the previous government. The bill as it then stood provided for the creation of the corporation which was to engage in insuring exports, with certain limitations on the risks. In addition the bill contained a very interesting feature in that under certain circumstances, upon the recommendation of the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Finance, the corporation could make direct loans to countries to which we might export goods.
In 1945 there was an amendment which provided for an increase in the lending provision whereby the amount the Canadian government could lend foreign governments for the purpose of buying exports from this country was increased to $750 million. This amount of money was lent to various countries, and I think the farsightedness of the government of that day in this treatment of our export trade certainly benefited Canada greatly. It was a remarkably successful policy.
Perhaps the best indication of just how sucessful this 1944-45 legislation was can be partially found in the fact that our total export trade in 1946 was about $4,266 million and by 1956 it had increased to about $10,574 million. This type of farsighted legislation was a help to exporters and at the same time helped other countries which were devastated in the war to re-establish their currencies so they could buy these exports. This policy certainly paid off for this country, if I may use such a phrase.
This act was amended from year to year. It was amended in 1946 to extend the risks that could be insured. It was amended in 1948 to permit the government to have the corporation, with the approval of the governor in council, make loans that were otherwise beyond the amount that the corporation would normally lend to any one exporter or to any one country. This provision was helpful and increased the development of the corporation. Then in 1954 there was a further amendment. One of the main things that amendment did was to increase the capital. In 1957 there was a rather useful amendment which extended the coverage so that in addition to insuring commodities and capital

goods, coverage could be provided for engineering services, goods sent out of the country for exhibition purposes and goods sent out of the country on consignment. In 1958 the present government further amended the bill to increase the amount of insurance the corporation could have outstanding at any one time. This amount was increased from $100 million to $200 million.
In his remarks this morning the minister, as I recall it, did not deal particularly with that phase of the matter. In view of the reasons he gave one year ago for asking for the increase in the liability the corporation could incur, and in view of the fact that he has come back so soon thereafter in effect to reduce the amount the corporation will have available for insurance purposes, I am wondering if the minister, when he closes this debate would clarify that point. In other words, this has been a very good piece of legislation, a very successful piece of legislation; yet the minister is in effect, by this bill, asking that the volume of business the corporation can do be reduced; that is in so far as the insurance aspect is concerned.

speechtext:
Because of the new purposes for which the gross amount may be spent. I ask the minister, therefore, if he would develop that point in his closing remarks at this stage of the legislation.
There are some other aspects of the bill to which I think the attention of the house should be drawn. Up to this point the scheme of the direction of the corporation has been by a statutory requirement that the Minister of Finance, the deputy minister of trade and commerce and the governor of the Bank of Canada be directors of the company and that four additional directors serve with them. I notice that this bill provides that the governor of the Bank of Canada be not included as a director of the corporation. The minister did not deal with that very important change. The corporation has been well directed and well run, and I for one am apprehensive as to the significance of the removal of the governor of the Bank of Canada from the board of directors of the corporation. I would hope the minister would clarify the reason for that change before we are asked to approve the principle.
There is another aspect of the bill before us. The minister carefully set out the need of exporters for financing in their operations; that is, as export trade has become more competitive there is a need for exporters to be able to give longer term credit to purchasers and this makes it difficult to finance their operations. I am in accord with his
Export Credits Insurance Act expression of the need in trade circles for that kind of assistance. This amendment puts the Export Credits Insurance Corporation into the business of buying, selling and guaranteeing the export paper, if I may use that term.
Now, we recently had before this house legislation setting up in Canada a corporation for the purpose of financing exports, discounting export paper if you will. I thought that legislation was particularly significant in our trade development, and very important. I should like to know whether the minister intends that this crown corporation should compete in the field of buying export paper with the export finance corporation recently set up by private legislation.
Then there is another aspect of this matter that concerns me. If I heard the minister correctly before the luncheon adjournment, I believe he said it was the intention to use the guarantee provisions of this bill only in cases where the amount of the transaction exceeded $250,000 and the term of the guarantee exceeded two years, I think I heard him correctly on that point.
That raises an interesting point. If we are to develop trade it is our total trade which must be developed. A very important factor there is not only the big exporters but the smaller manufacturing exporters in particular, because the expansion must come in that area as well as in the area referred to by the minister. In dealing with the minister's estimates a few days ago I raised a matter in connection with that point and asked him to examine the possibility of taking measures that would assist exporters, particularly the smaller exporters, in the very large potential market in the United States. I am sorry to see him limit the new legislation to what I might describe in general terms as big business. It seems to me that the need for financing is just as great in the smaller industrial business in Canada as it is in the big industrial business and if you are to legislate on this particular subject we should provide for all our manufacturers and exporters the benefit of the assistance or facilities we are providing. That distinction made by the minister seemed to be quite unrealistic.
There is one other criticism I have of this measure. I have spoken in rather enthusiastic terms of the present act, the Export Credits Insurance Act. Indeed, some members would think I had been very laudatory of the farsightedness of the former government in bringing it in, and I have spoken of the great benefits it has brought to this country. I for one am sorry to see the minister now come forward with legislation which will divert that corporation from its

Export Credits Insurance Act main purpose of insuring the exports of this country. It seems to me that the corporation has functioned well. There is such a need for continuation of the insurance of export credits that it is unfortunate that this legislation has provided for what in effect is an entirely new business namely the guaranteeing of export paper, or the actual buying and selling of the export instruments being done through this corporation. I would have thought if the crown were to engage in that business it should have done it by a separate corporation, because it is a separate function altogether.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO DELETE REFERENCE TO GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA, TO EXTEND APPLICATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext:
That is really embarking upon an operation similar to that of the export-import bank of the United States referred to by my colleague from Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson), and it is another field altogether. As a matter of fact, I am not sure whether the corporation should be wholly a crown corporation or whether the crown has explored the possibility of bringing more private enterprise into this field. However, I am in complete accord with the need for action in this field at this time.
I do hope the minister has considered that point thoroughly, and if he has that he will explain more fully to the house why he chose this approach to the problem rather than making provision by separate legislation for a separate corporation, because it is really a new field. It is an international commercial banking operation in which the minister is now engaging.
There is another problem about the bill which is before us. I do not know to what extent I may refer to proceedings in the other place, but when this bill was before a committee in the other place it became apparent from the explanations given that what was intended, although the bill does not provide this, was mainly the guaranteeing of export credit paper, and that this would facilitate the exporters' financing of that paper once it was guaranteed. While there is no explanation as to how that was to be facilitated, it is self-evident that it will facilitate it to some extent; but in a period of tight money-I hope not to get into further argument with the Minister of Finance on this particular aspect of it and using that term in the sense that the commercial banks, by reason of bond holdings and for other reasons have not large sums of money available for lending purposes- it is difficult to see how the mere guaranteeing of the paper will particularly assist the exporter to finance through the banks.


Therefore I think if the guarantee aspect of the proposal is to be successful the minister ought to explain to us a little more fully how it is to be successful, because in a tight money period it is not necessarily the security of the loan which is the problem with the commercial banks, but the availability of funds to loan.
A second point in that connection is the long term of the guarantee. The Canadian banks, which are both commercial banks and savings banks combined, have always sought to keep very large portions of their funds in short term securities or loans. They have been very careful about that and have done a very good job over the years. This legislation provides only for the guaranteeing of long term paper. If that is so, then this measure is not going to help the exporters finance through the banks. That again leads us to the question, in what way, then, is a long term export paper guarantee going to help the exporter to finance?
Then there is the whole operation of the buying and selling of the paper. Notwithstanding what was said in the committee in the other place, where the whole emphasis was laid on the guaranteeing of the paper rather than on the matter of buying and selling the paper, I am still of the opinion that the corporation is going to find itself in the position of buying and selling large quantities of these guaranteed instruments. I noticed that in his remarks this morning the minister said relatively little about the buying and selling of such paper but a great deal about the guaranteeing of it. If the corporation is to engage in this commercial banking operation of buying and selling such paper, then surely if that is to become the main purpose of the legislation it is another operation altogether from the insuring of risks.
Those are questions which are outstanding in my mind, Mr. Speaker, which I hope the minister will deal with at some length. While he will see that I have been critical of the bill, I am wholly in accord with the purpose sought to be served by the bill and the minister's assessment of the need for some sort of assistance to exporters.
Before I conclude my remarks I must just add one further thing which I think ought to be said. I appreciate very much the minister acknowledging the honour which has been done to Canada by the election of the president of our Export Credits Insurance Corporation to be head of the Berne union. This is an acknowledgment of the splendid services of that officer, and it is also a courtesy and an honour to this country that I am happy to join in acknowledging.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO DELETE REFERENCE TO GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA, TO EXTEND APPLICATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are pleased that this bill has been introduced, because not only does it seek to continue the Export Credits Insurance Act but it also provides amendments for the purpose of expanding the activities of that corporation.
Canada at this time is facing serious difficulties in the export of a great many commodities. We realize that we are facing difficulties in the export of lead and zinc, copper, wheat and oil, although the difficulties in that direction seem to have been lessening in recent days because of actions taken by the United States government. Nevertheless, with regard to a great many commodities Canada is finding export sales increasingly difficult to obtain.
We are all aware that the Soviet union is engaged in a growing trade offensive, but that country does not have to rely in any sense upon private institutions to make commercial transactions in the commodities available for export. Rather, the Soviet union is able to enter the market by means of long term contracts and by means of credits at very low rates of interest which enable her to undercut markets which might otherwise be those of Canada or of some other western nations. Private enterprise in the ordinary sense of those words is unable to compete with this growing expansion in world trade on the part of the Soviet union.
We see extraordinary statements made from time to time by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and by leading businessmen in this country advocating an expansion of public credit to enable corporations to develop their business in the export field. As a matter of fact, the measure now before us is a good socialist measure. It provides a public corporation to undertake business which private enterprise is either unwilling or unable to engage in. Those who wish to put forward their private enterprise views will say, of course, that this is merely a measure to assist ordinary business establishments. subtopic: AMENDMENT TO DELETE REFERENCE TO GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA, TO EXTEND APPLICATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to speak at length in connection with this measure because the views of this party were very well expressed by the hon. member for Ottawa West.
This amendment represents an extension of the field of government participation from insurance to finance to encourage our exports, and I am sure all hon. members of the house would approve of that objective. I share with the hon. member for Ottawa West curiosity as to how this function can be reconciled with the initiation of private enterprise in this field, as evinced by legislation which we have had before us during the current session. In addition, if this is likely to be an impressive field I share with the hon. member a desire to question the minister as to why we are including in an insurance act this additional function which seems to be so closely related to the export-import bank function of our neighbour to the south.

That raises a question as to why, if this is to foe an impressive function, this bill does not in any way increase the total financial liability under the act, which was set at a maximum of $200 million. If the government is to go into a new field, and if this new field is to accomplish anything, surely it cannot be accomplished solely by endorsing a certain amount of paper without requiring over a period of operation an actual requirement for financial resources. No request has been made for an increase in financial resources.
I note from the annual report that the liabilities under section 21 of the act were $51 million and those under section 13 were $84 million as at December 31, 1958. I do not think the minister brought us up to date as to the current position with respect to liabilities particularly under section 21, and I wish he would do so.
This bill was introduced in the other place. The banking and commerce committee of the other place examined Mr. A. W. Thomas, assistant general manager of the Export Credits Insurance Corporation, who in his initial statement to that body on Wednesday, June 10, 1959, as reported at page 7 of the evidence of the committee, said:
-the substance of the hill is in this matter of guarantee. The responsibility is going to be taken by the government and not by the corporation, for we are an insurance corporation.
I believe that highlights the suggestion of the hon. member for Ottawa West that if the statute we are now amending is essentially related to insurance, there is some merit in thinking about the possibility of separating the two functions. That would not be done here and I do not think we propose to divide the house on that point, but I feel that the minister should consider the advantages of there being two acts providing for a separation of functions, particularly when the assistant general manager of the company asserts that decisions with respect to matters of this kind are going to be government decisions rather than decisions of the corporation itself.
Another question that has concerned me in connection with the new sphere of activity suggested under this bill is related to our knowledge that in the insurance realm we have had coinsurance. On the same page of the proceedings of the banking and commerce committee of the other place Mr. Thomas said:
The policy of insurance-
That has hitherto been the function of the corporation.
-is subjected to terms and conditions and to a co-insurance which is normally-[DOT]

I want to emphasize the word "normally". I continue:
-not in excess of 85 per cent of any loss which might be suffered by the exporter-
I was curious about the word "normal". Have there been policies of insurance undertaken by the corporation where the coinsurance by the exporter was less than 15 per cent? In addition I would ask the minister to tell us today or on a subsequent occasion when we are debating the clauses of the bill how guarantees are going to fit into the traditional experience of coinsurance. With respect to endorsing a promissory note, for instance, does the minister conceive that he can endorse or guarantee that paper on a percentage basis rather than in entirety as to the face value of the paper guaranteed? I think there is great merit in retaining an interest on the part of the exporter in repayment and the proper eventual success of the transaction. I am wondering whether or not under this form of financing the corporation is likely to get into the position of being 100 per cent interested, without a co-interest on the part of the exporter himself.
We have some knowledge, of course, as to the competitive position that Canada is in which necessitates and makes desirable legislation of this kind. In the matter of down payments, what is the likely requirement in the view of the minister in this respect? I understand that with respect to insurance facilities in the United States a down payment there is required where the cover will not exceed 60 per cent. What is the minister's advice to his corporation in this respect? In so far as rates are concerned, is the minister contemplating that rates of insurance will continue to be standard without differentiation with respect to individual transactions? I believe there is now something in the nature of a trade union among government export insurers, and the firm convention provides for a maximum term of loan contracts of five years. There are some countries at least that are competitors of ours which do not belong to this association, notably Italy, and there are some others.
What is the possibility of getting competitors of this kind into the Berne organization? Notwithstanding the Berne convention and agreements I believe that in the United States, by virtue of the export-import bank, an extremely important competitor there has an opportunity to assist exports by means of development loans. I think this avoids the Berne agreement to the extent that these development loans could be for a term of as long as 20 years. Does that not appeal to
Export Credits Insurance Act the minister as an additional reason for perhaps separating the financing and putting that in a separate statute, such as is the case in the United States, rather than including it in a statute that is basically an export credit insurance act?
The minister, of course, will be very well aware of the fact that Germany has been extremely aggressive in this field and through its reconstruction loan corporation is a competitor. I question whether it is desirable that we be in the Berne agreement with respect to credit insurance and have terms that might be related to insurance in some way interpreted by our friendly competitors in other countries as being bound as a result of that statute, whereas they are really finance matters which these other countries have handled by separate statutes and separate organizations, notably the Export-Import bank of the United States.

My understanding is that the corporation will guarantee the exporter unconditionally for the full amount of his account. That has not been true heretofore. Mr. Speaker, on the first point raised by the hon. member for Ottawa West may I say that I think it is based on a misunderstanding, perhaps owing to a reply I gave to a question he asked me just at one o'clock. I misunderstood his question.


He asked me whether there was any limitation on the amount of guaranteed export paper, if you can use that term, which might be bought and I said no. But as he indicated in the course of his remarks, the proposed amendment under section 21B states as follows:
21B. (1) The aggregate of
(a)	the liability of the corporation under contracts of insurance entered into under section 21 and outstanding, and

shall not at any time exceed two hundred million dollars, . . .

speechtext:
That was one of the two
points I raised. You see, the present act provides for insuring export credits. That is the purpose of the act. The new bill provides for guaranteeing, buying and selling instruments. Instruments are a different thing altogether from what is insured. "Instrument" is defined in the bill as a promissory note, bill of exchange and so on. It is discount paper. It is a wholly new operation distinct from the business of insurance of contracts for the payment for export commodities and capital goods. Therefore my first point is that the procedure is not in accordance with section 54 of the British North America Act because the purpose of the bill is wholly new. The bill undoubtedly creates a charge because guaranteeing up to $200 million is admittedly a charge, so even if the total liability is not increased the purpose is wholly new. That was the first point.
The second point was a little different.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO DELETE REFERENCE TO GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA, TO EXTEND APPLICATION OF ACT, ETC.

It is the second point that concerns me. I think the first point can be and has been answered by the reference to May. The general purpose of the appropriation of $200 million is the facilitation of export trade, in the old bill by insurance and in the new bill by insurance plus the guaranteeing of instruments. Therefore I think that point is perhaps not worth pursuing, subject to what authorities the hon. member
Export Credits Insurance Act may cite, but the second point is one on which I should like to be satisfied, namely that the buying of instruments is also limited to the $200 million.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO DELETE REFERENCE TO GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA, TO EXTEND APPLICATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext:
I have stated my first point and I am not going to press it unduly at the moment. But Your Honour can see how far we could go astray by permitting the introduction of a wholly new purpose in an amending bill. If you had an act respecting housing, then instead of introducing new legislation the government could change the purpose and build railroads with the amount of money voted for housing. I will not develop that argument further but I thought it should be raised.
My second point is that the total liability that can be a charge on the public funds at any one time under section 21 of the existing act is $200 million. That is the maximum amount of liability outstanding at any one time. The act uses the expression, "shall not at any time exceed $200 million". The new legislation provides for the corporation engaging in three new activities that are different from insurance. As I submitted in my previous argument, they are wholly different in purpose. They are the guaranteeing of promissory notes, bills of exchange and other negotiable instruments, the buying of such instruments and the selling of such instruments. The limit of liability in the new bill will be found at the bottom of page 2 where it says that the liability of the importers under all outstanding guaranteed instruments-that is just the liability of the guarantees outstanding at any one time-shall not, together with the existing liability under the act, exceed $200 million so that the amount is the same $200 million. However there is no limitation whatever under the buying provision.
Let me take an example of what could be done under the bill in order to illustrate my point. Assume that the bill is passed and next month we guarantee paper to the extent of $200 million. They can then buy all the guaranteed negotiable instruments. They can buy and sell; they can incur a loss, but the continuing guarantee stays at $200 million, that is clear. It is limited. However, in the buying and selling they can buy guaranteed paper and incur a loss on it by selling, which loss would be a charge on the taxpayer. This buying and selling operation is a trading operation and it is not limited to the $200 million.
If we could reduce an example to an absurdity in order to illustrate the point, Mr. Speaker, I would say they could buy $200 million of guaranteed paper and next month sell it for $190 million. Then they could come right back and guarantee $200

Export Credits Insurance Act million worth of paper, so that the charge on the treasury would then become $210 million at the end of the month.

If the corporation then buys that instrument it is not adding anything to the liabilities of the corporation, but is presumably replacing its liability for the guarantee of the debt. I am inclined to think that the minister's advice was sound. It is always difficult to know with these bills which authorize complicated transactions, whether or not new money is involved. I think that the argument is really concluded by section 2 IB which defines how the $200 million already authorized by parliament can be applied in the future. It can be applied to existing purposes of the corporation, that is the liability of the corporation under contracts of insurance entered into under section 21 and -not or-the liability of importers under all outstanding guaranteed instruments. In effect, therefore, this bill divides the $200 million already authorized between the old purpose and the new purpose and to that extent it cuts down the amount available for insurance and makes some part of the $200 million available to guarantee the liability of importers.
Now, let us look at the guarantee provisions. The corporation may purchase guaranteed instruments under subsection 2 of section 21 A, and if you look at what a guaranteed instrument is you will find it means an instrument the payment of which is guaranteed by the corporation under this section. What the corporation, in effect, is doing is purchasing its own guarantee, and to that extent it does not increase the liability of the corporation which is already limited to $200 million because the instrument which it has guaranteed is an instrument of liability of some importer. have been impressed, as I am sure all the rest of us have been with the success of this corporation over the ensuing years. I have already explained what we intend to do.
